Discussion
Schistosomiasis mansoni remains a significant public health concern in Brazil,
particularly in regions with precarious socio -environmental conditions. The state of
Alagoas, located in the Northeast region of the country, continues to present active
transmission foci despite decades of control programs.3 In the epidemiological context of
Feira Grande, an area classified as low -endemicity, the results of this study highlighted
important limitations of both traditionally recommended diagnostic methods and current
protocols, especially in low-intensity infection settings.
Both the WHO recommendation (two KK slides) and the Brazilian national
guideline (six KK slides) underestimated the true positivity rate of schistosomiasis in this
low-endemicity area, with positivity rates of 4.7% and 8.8%, respectively, compared to
17.9% identified by the reference standard. The molecular technique demonstrated a
sensitivity of 84.2% and almost perfect agreement, surpassing even the 16 -slide KK
protocol, which reached a sensitivity of 70.2%. This performance reinforces the role of
PCR in detecting low-intensity infections, as also reported by other studies.16,17
These findings underscore the limitation of KK in areas where infections tend to
occur at low intensities. Previous studies have already indicated that, despite its simplicity
and low cost, KK exhibits low sensitivity in low -endemicity settings, especially when
applied with a limited number of slides .18–20 The current strategy recommended by the
Brazilian Ministry of Health achieved a sensitivity of 49.1%, higher than that obtained
with the WHO protocol (26.3%), but still failed to diagnose nearly half of the cases. The
use of 16 slides provided a more accurate estimate of the true positivity rate a nd showed
progressive gains up to the 12th slide, with subsequent stabilization, suggesting a balance
point between diagnostic performance and operational feasibility. In this context, our
study stands out by presenting an expanded and innovative approach, offering a more
sensitive and robust alternative for estimating the true infection positivity in the studied
population.

Most individuals diagnosed in this study exhibited low parasite loads, consistent
with the epidemiological transition observed in Brazil’s endemic areas over recent
decades.1 This profile aligns with the scenario expected by the WHO for regions where
control strategies are well established.10 However, despite representing progress, this
pattern poses new challenges for epidemiological surveillance and diagnosis. The
predominance of low -intensity infections reduces the sensitivity of parasitological
methods, including KK, primarily when performed with a limited number of slides .11,21
Other studies have shown that such methods may significantly underestimate the true
schistosomiasis positivity in low-endemicity areas, leading to the omission of mild cases
that remain untreated and serve as silent reservoirs of the parasite.20,22,23 This diagnostic
failure directly compromises the effectiveness of surveillance and control strategies by
underestimating the true magnitude of infection and fostering a false perception of
control. Furthermore, in contex ts of high socio -environmental vulnerability and
discontinuities in public health policies, these scenarios may favor disease reemergence
and a return to high transmission patterns.24
The introduction of PCR as a complementary diagnostic tool enabled the
identification of additional infected individuals who were not detected even after the
analysis of 16 KK slides. The effectiveness of PCR for schistosomiasis diagnosis has been
previously demonstrated, highlighting its ability to detect minimal amounts of parasite
genetic material, even in cases of low -intensity infection .7,25,26 This reinforces the
limitations of traditional parasitological methods , which, although highly specific, lack
sensitivity in low -parasite-load contexts. Despite the higher cost of PCR posing a
challenge for routine implementation in public health systems, the cost of materials
required for six KK slides, as currently recommended by the Brazilian Ministry of Health,
is comparable and may offer more sensitive diagnostic outcomes.17 From this perspective,
the strategic and targeted use of PCR in low -endemicity areas or regions with suspected
underreporting may strengthen epidemiological surveillance.
The socioeconomic profile of the study population heightens the epidemiological
significance of these findings . The predominance of infected individuals with low
education levels, low income, and poor sanitation , including the use of untreated well
water and open sewage, creates a setting conducive to the persistence of schistosomiasis
and soil-transmitted helminth infections. This was also reflected in the high prevalence
of Ancylostomidae (18.7%). Furthermore, the local economy, primarily based on small-
scale farming of sweet potatoes, cassava, and tobacco .27 requires frequent contact with

water bodies, increasing the risk of exposure to S. mansoni infective stages. This risk is
further exacerbated by the documented presence of breeding sites for Biomphalaria
glabrata and B. straminea, the intermediate hosts of the parasite in the region .13 Taken
together, these factors illustrate an endemic scenari o sustained by socio -environmental
vulnerabilities, emphasizing the urgent need for integrated control strategies that
prioritize improved sanitation and accurate diagnosis.
Beyond technical limitations, the current schistosomiasis landscape in Brazil is
further complicated by structural issues. The decentralization of surveillance and control
activities, insufficient resource allocation to the Schistosomiasis Control Program, and
shortcomings in information system reporting hinder accurate disease monitor ing.
Previous studies have indicated significant underreporting within the Schistosomiasis
Control Program Information System, particularly in areas with low primary healthcare
coverage or logistical challenges .28–30 This underreporting contributes to a false
perception of control and allows active transmission foci to persist. However, despite
these limitations, data from official information systems, alongside mandatory case
reporting and research initiatives employing more sensitive diagnostic tools, such as this
study, have helped to construct a more realistic picture of the epidemiological status of
schistosomiasis in the country.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the results of this study showed that combining multiple KK slides
with PCR significantly improves diagnostic accuracy for detecting schistosomiasis
mansoni in low -endemicity areas, compared to the isolated use of KK with a limited
number of slides. The performance analysis of the strate gies currently recommended by
the WHO and the Brazilian Ministry of Health revealed that, although the latter represents
progress over previous guidelines, it still presents significant limitations in settings with
low parasite burdens. The limited sensitivity of KK, especially when based on a reduced
number of slides, leads to underdiagnosis, hindering case identification and treatment and
compromising the interruption of the transmission cycle. Therefore, the adoption of
locally adapted, more sensitive, a nd integrated diagnostic protocols is essential to
improve infection detection capacity, enhance surveillance activities, and ensure the
effectiveness of strategies aimed at eliminating schistosomiasis mansoni as a public
health problem, in line with the WHO targets for 2030.
